## Introduction

We have looked at `vectors`, and `matrices`. Now we will see how these two views of number-arrays coalesce and come together in the form of `linear transformations`. This will allow us to conceptualize the idea of shapes created using vectors can be morphed based on *where we stand* and how a POV is everything in Space.

## Basis Vectors in a Matrix?

Recollect our definion of `vectors` and the related ideas of `components` and `coordinates`. We saw that a vector can be represented as a linear combination of basis vectors. 

$$
\overrightarrow{a} = a_x \hat{i} + a_y \hat{j}
$${#eq-vector-basis}

Now, since $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ are *themselves vectors*, we should be able to write `coordinates` and `components` for them!! Can we, for example, in 2D space, the standard `basis vectors` do this?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
\hat{i} = \mathbf{e_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad\\
\\
\hat{j} = \mathbf{e_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
$$
:::

::: {.column width="10%"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Unit Vectors](index_files/figure-html/fig-unit-vectors-1.png){#fig-unit-vectors fig-align='center' width=75%}
:::
:::

:::

::::

Now, if we stack the basis vectors $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ as columns of a matrix, we get the `identity matrix`:

$$
I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$${#eq-identity-matrix}

And, finally merging `vectors` and `matrices` into one view, we can ***represent the vector*** as a matrix multiplication of `coordinates` and `basis vectors`:

$$
\begin{align}
\overrightarrow{a} &= a_x \hat{i} + a_y \hat{j}\\
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_x \\ a_y \end{bmatrix}
\end{align}
$${#eq-vectors-matrix-mult}

Of course we expected this; what else can an `identity matrix` do for us, other than tell us what things are? But now let us see if we can mess with the `identity matrix`, and see what happens to the vector $\overrightarrow{a}$. And what it really means to the `frame of reference` and the `point of view` in space.

## Into the Matrix: Changing Identity and Space

Suppose, instead of the `identity matrix`, we use a different matrix, say:
$$
I_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
and we naively carry out the matrix multiplication as before, @eq-vectors-matrix-mult):

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

$$
\begin{align}
\overrightarrow{a_2} &= I_2 \begin{bmatrix} a_x \\ a_y \end{bmatrix} \\
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_x \\ a_y \end{bmatrix}\\
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 a_x \\ a_y \end{bmatrix}
\end{align}
$${#eq-vectors-matrix-mult-2}

:::
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Vector morphed by a Matrix](index_files/figure-html/fig-morph-1-1.png){#fig-morph-1 fig-align='center' width=75%}
:::
:::

:::

::::

What hath God wrought?[^1] It should be immediately apparent that we have *morphed* the vector $\overrightarrow{a}$ into a new vector $\overrightarrow{a_2}$, which is twice as long in the $x$-direction, but unchanged in the $y$-direction. 

[AND: we have a new `vector space` where the `basis vectors` have been transformed from $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ to $\hat{i_2}$ and $\hat{j_2}$ !!]{style="background-color:yellow;"}. **We have morphed and transformed space itself**!

::: callout-important
## Morphed Identity Matrices morph Space itself
This is serious business and an undeniable super-power! A matrix represents in concise form a `transformation`, a `function`, that takes `vector`s as input and gives us new `vectors`. 
It does so by changing the `basis vectors`. We have changed the [`alphabet`](../20-Vectors/index.qmd#vector-spaces) of the `vector space` itself, and hence the `coordinates` of the `vectors` in that space.
:::

## Wait,  But Why?

- Matrices are a representation of *linear transformations*.
- *Linear Transformations* are functions that take `vectors` as input and give us new `vectors` as output.
- The matrix is a compact representation of the `transformation``, and it tells us how the `basis vectors` are transformed.
- When we multiply a vector by a matrix, we are applying the `transformation` to that `vector`, which results in a new `vector` in the transformed space.
- A `transformation` is a `matrix` that contains *transformed* `basis vectors`. These guys change first, and then chamge everything else. 
- This is a powerful concept because it allows us to manipulate and understand geometric transformations in a linear algebraic framework.
- Algebra and Geometry are not that far apart!!

## Conclusion

- Understanding `matrix multiplication` as a morphing of `unit basis vectors` provides a powerful visualization method.
- As artists and designers, we can **design** transformations by imagining 2D space as a rubber sheet, and then stretching, compressing, shearing, or rotating it to see how vectors change.
- The idea of *changing basis vectors* also applies to space in higher dimensions, which is what is done inside [neural networks](../../100-AI/10-NeuralNets/index.qmd) and other machine learning algorithms.
